input.question: How do new species arise?
input.ground_truth: Evolution is the very gradual change in genes over time. It isn't that one day an organism gave birth to a human. Rather, it's that over a several thousand year span, creatures stopped being a human ancestor and were instead human. There is no absolute point.

Question: How do new species arise?

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a bunch of puppies in a big yard. Some puppies look a little different from each other—maybe one has really floppy ears, and another has a curly tail. 

Now, when those puppies grow up and have their own puppies, sometimes their special features (like floppy ears or curly tails) get passed on to the new puppies. Over a *very* long time, if a group of puppies with curly tails only play and have puppies with other curly-tailed puppies, after many, many generations, all their puppies will have curly tails and be different from the puppies with floppy ears.

That’s how new kinds of puppies (or any animals, or plants!) can appear. Little changes add up over a long time, and after many generations, you can have a whole new group that is different enough to be called a new "species." It’s like a family tree that changes so much that it becomes a totally new kind of tree!
